title: Ki Tavo: this day (Deuteronomy 26:16, 27:9)
hook: Rashi: let the commandments feel new each day, as if given today
tomorrow: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, arami oved avi, the farmer's story. Your line was a wandering father. Today, two small words Moses keeps repeating.

Remember the last time something was new. A phone with the plastic still on the screen. The first day at a job, when you noticed every hallway. A friendship in its first weeks, when every message felt important. Now picture the same thing a year later. The phone is scratched. The hallways are invisible. The messages are routine. Nothing changed but your eyes. Moses is speaking to a people who have lived with God's commandments for forty years. And he keeps calling it today.
screen: `THE PLASTIC ON THE SCREEN.` → `A YEAR LATER: INVISIBLE.` → `FORTY YEARS, AND CALLED TODAY.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy twenty-six, verse sixteen: "This day the LORD thy God commandeth thee to do these statutes and ordinances." This day. But many of these laws had been given at Sinai, long before. A chapter later, Moses and the priests say: "Keep silence, and hear, O Israel; this day thou art become a people unto the LORD thy God." They'd been a people for four decades. In Hebrew, the word is hayom: today. Rashi, the great eleventh-century commentator from France, reads it as an instruction about how to hold something old. On the first verse he says, in effect: every day these commandments should be in your eyes as new, as though you'd been commanded them that very day. On the second: each day, see yourself as if you had entered the covenant today. It's a teaching about attention. The danger in a long practice usually isn't rebellion. It's autopilot: the prayer you can say without hearing it, the blessing muttered on the way to the first bite, the person across the table you've stopped really seeing. Rashi doesn't say pretend it's new. He says let it be new in your eyes. The text stays the same; the eyes are the part that can change. Jewish life is full of repetition built on this hope: the same prayers every morning, the same Torah read every year, and an expectation that this time something in them will catch you differently. Hayom. Not a date on a calendar. A way of looking.
screen: `HAYOM: THIS DAY.` · `FORTY YEARS OLD, CALLED TODAY.` · `RASHI: NEW IN YOUR EYES.` · `THE TEXT STAYS; THE EYES CHANGE.` · then, large: `THIS DAY, NEW.`

segments.voice: Choose something you do so often you've stopped noticing it: a blessing, a greeting, the way you make tea, saying goodnight to someone. Walk through it slowly in your mind, as if for the first time, and ask what a stranger would notice. Find one detail you'd stopped seeing, and hold it in view.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. And in it, hayom: this day, said about things that were already old.
Your line: this day, new. The same old words, read with fresh eyes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rashi's reading of 'this day' is often taught as the reason a daily prayer or weekly Torah portion should not become routine; many teachers ask students to find something new in a familiar text each time it comes around.
